title: Upper Volta Gains Independence from France
note: Upper Volta became independent on August 5, 1960, with Maurice Yaméogo of the UDV-RDA as first president. All core facts confirmed.

title: Yaméogo Establishes Single-Party State Under UDV
note: Yaméogo banned opposition parties shortly after independence and created a single-party state under the UDV-RDA. Confirmed by multiple sources.

title: Austerity Budget Sparks Protests Against Yaméogo
note: Salary cuts and austerity sparked mass protests by trade unions and workers in 1965, culminating in the January 1966 coup. Year is consistent with the buildup to the coup.

title: First Military Coup — Lamizana Overthrows Yaméogo
note: Coup occurred on January 3, 1966; General Sangoulé Lamizana seized power in a bloodless coup amid mass protests. All core facts confirmed.

title: Lamizana Restores Partial Civilian Government
note: Lamizana oversaw a new constitution and hybrid civilian-military governance from 1969–1970. Year is correct for the beginning of this transition phase.

title: Lamizana Dissolves Government — Returns to Full Military Rule
note: On February 8, 1974, Lamizana dissolved the National Assembly and suspended the constitution in a self-coup, returning to full military rule. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: New Constitution Approved — Multiparty Elections Held
note: Constitution approved by referendum in November 1977; multiparty presidential elections held in May 1978 with Lamizana winning. Year 1977 is correct for the constitution.

title: Coup Removes Lamizana — Colonel Zerbo Takes Power
note: On November 25, 1980, Colonel Saye Zerbo led a bloodless coup ousting Lamizana. All core facts confirmed.

title: Second Coup of the Year — Ouédraogo Replaces Zerbo
note: On November 7, 1982, a coup removed Zerbo and installed Major Jean-Baptiste Ouédraogo. The title says 'second coup of the year' but it was the only coup in 1982, not a second of the year. However the event itself (date, names, year) is correct.

title: Sankara Revolution — Radical Coup Transforms Upper Volta
note: On August 4, 1983, Sankara with Compaoré's support overthrew Ouédraogo and launched a revolutionary government. Sankara was 33. All core facts confirmed.

title: Upper Volta Renamed Burkina Faso — New Identity Proclaimed
note: On August 4, 1984 (first anniversary of the revolution), Sankara renamed the country Burkina Faso. All facts confirmed including the meaning and date.

title: Sankara's Social Revolution — Health, Education, and Women's Rights
note: Mass vaccinations, compulsory education, women's rights advances, and austerity for officials are all documented aspects of Sankara's 1983–1987 revolution; year 1984 is representative of peak implementation.

title: Sankara Confronts Traditional Chiefs and IMF — Rejects Dependency
note: Sankara's land redistribution from chiefs and public defiance of IMF structural adjustment are well-documented features of his rule. Year 1984 as label for his revolutionary tenure is reasonable.

title: Brief Border War with Mali Over Agacher Strip
note: Five-day war ran December 25–30, 1985. Casualties ranged from 59 to 300. ICJ divided territory in 1986. All core facts confirmed; description says 'hundreds of casualties' which is consistent with the upper range of estimates.

title: Sankara Assassinated — Compaoré Seizes Power
note: Sankara killed October 15, 1987, along with 12 aides, in a coup led by Compaoré. All core facts confirmed.

title: Compaoré's 'Rectification' — Revolution Reversed
note: Compaoré's 'rectification' dismantled Sankara's program, restored market policies, and reopened IMF negotiations. Year 1988 as the first full year of reversal is consistent with sources.

title: Compaoré Represses Internal Dissent and Coup Attempt
note: September 1989 alleged coup plot by Lingani and Zongo; both were summarily executed. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: Multiparty Constitution Approved — Compaoré Civilianizes Rule
note: Constitution adopted June 2, 1991 by referendum; Compaoré won December 1991 election with opposition boycott. All core facts confirmed.

title: Clement Ouédraogo Assassination Silences Opposition
note: Clément Oumarou Ouédraogo was killed in 1991 by a grenade explosion in his car; the case was never officially resolved. Year and basic facts confirmed.

title: CFA Franc Devaluation Shocks Economy
note: CFA franc devalued 50% in January 1994; impacted all member countries including Burkina Faso. Year and percentage confirmed.

title: Compaoré's ODP-MT Dominates Flawed Elections
note: The ODP-MT was merged into the new CDP party in February 1996; the legislative elections that delivered a CDP majority occurred in 1997, not 1996. Year is off by one year.

title: Journalist Norbert Zongo Murdered — Press Freedom Crisis
note: Zongo and three companions were found shot and burned on December 13, 1998 near Sapouy. All core facts confirmed including his newspaper and the David Ouédraogo connection.

title: Mass Protests Over Zongo Killing Shake Compaoré Regime
note: Sustained protests throughout 1999 following Zongo's December 1998 killing are well documented. Year and political impact confirmed.

title: Constitutional Amendments Impose Presidential Term Limits
note: 2000 constitutional amendment imposed two-term presidential limits; Constitutional Council later ruled it non-retroactive. Year and facts confirmed.

title: Coup Plot Uncovered — Army Loyalists Arrested
note: October 2003 alleged coup plot led to arrests of military officers and civilians. Year and basic facts confirmed.

title: Compaoré Re-elected in Disputed Vote — Opposition Boycotts
note: Compaoré won 80.35% of votes in 2005; significant opposition candidates did participate (it was not a full boycott but opposition was fragmented), and Compaoré ran by overriding the term-limit amendment. Core facts on year and result confirmed.

title: ECOWAS Mediator Role — Compaoré Brokers Regional Peace Deals
note: Compaoré was a recognized regional mediator for Côte d'Ivoire, Mali, Niger, and Togolese crises. Year 2007 used as representative label for his peak mediation period is consistent with sources.

title: Food Price Riots Rock Ouagadougou
note: Riots in late February 2008 over food price spikes; Ouagadougou was affected along with other cities. All core facts confirmed.

title: Military Mutinies and Urban Riots Shake Compaoré Government
note: Series of military mutinies from February–June 2011 over unpaid allowances, concurrent with civilian protests. Compaoré sacked government and army hierarchy. All core facts confirmed.

title: Cotton Sector Crisis — Smallholder Farmers in Distress
note: Burkina Faso's cotton sector faced structural challenges in this period, but a specific crisis peaking in 2012 with the exact characteristics described (debt accumulation, price below production costs) could not be confirmed from available sources.

title: Gold Mining Revenues Surge — New Economic Pillar Established
note: Gold surpassed cotton as Burkina Faso's leading export in approximately 2009, not 2013. By 2013 gold dominance was already well established. Year is off.

title: Popular Uprising Ousts Compaoré After 27 Years
note: October 30–31, 2014 uprising against Compaoré's constitutional amendment attempt; parliament burned, Compaoré fled to Côte d'Ivoire after 27 years. All core facts confirmed.

title: Transitional Military Government Quickly Yields to Civilian Council
note: Lt. Col. Isaac Zida briefly assumed power before ECOWAS-mediated transition to Michel Kafando as interim president. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: RSP Coup Attempt — Presidential Guard Seizes Government
note: RSP seized transitional government on September 16–17, 2015, arresting Kafando and Zida. Regular army forced RSP to stand down within days. All core facts confirmed.

title: RSP Dissolved — Presidential Guard Dismantled
note: RSP was disbanded after the failed September 2015 coup attempt. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: Roch Marc Christian Kaboré Elected President
note: Kaboré won November 2015 presidential election with 53.49% first-round, first non-interim president without military ties in 49 years. All core facts confirmed.

title: Jihadist Attack on Splendid Hotel and Cappuccino Café — Ouagadougou
note: Attack on January 15–16, 2016 killed at least 30 people from multiple nationalities. Claimed by AQIM and al-Mourabitoun (not JNIM, which was formed later). Minor label discrepancy but year and core facts confirmed.

title: Sankara Assassination Case Reopened — Justice Sought
note: An arrest warrant was issued against Compaoré in March 2016 following reopening of the case post-2014. Year and facts confirmed.

title: Jihadist Violence Spreads from North — Sahel Region Deteriorates
note: Jihadist groups extended operations into Sahel and Est regions from 2017 onward; mass displacement began. Year and trajectory confirmed.

title: G5 Sahel Joint Force Launched — Regional Security Alliance
note: G5 Sahel Joint Force authorized by African Union in April 2017 and by UN Security Council in June 2017. Burkina Faso was a founding member. All core facts confirmed.

title: French Embassy and Military HQ Attacked in Ouagadougou
note: Coordinated attacks on March 2, 2018 targeted the French Embassy and Burkina Faso military HQ. Official toll was 8 security forces killed, though other reports suggest higher numbers. Year confirmed.

title: Church and School Massacres — Sectarian Violence Escalates
note: Wave of attacks on Catholic churches and Christians in northern Burkina Faso in 2019, with dozens killed and schools forced to close. Year and key facts confirmed.

title: Humanitarian Crisis Deepens — Over 500,000 Internally Displaced
note: By October 2019, IDP numbers reached approximately 486,000–500,000 depending on source and date. Year and approximate figure confirmed.

title: Kaboré Re-elected Amid Deepening Insecurity
note: Kaboré won re-election November 22, 2020 with 57.87% (approximately 58%); voting was impossible in conflict-affected areas. All core facts confirmed.

title: Solhan Massacre — 160 Civilians Killed in Village Attack
note: Attack on Solhan village, Yagha province, June 4–5, 2021. At least 160 killed, deadliest massacre in Burkina Faso's insurgency at that point. All core facts confirmed.

title: IDP Crisis Surpasses 1.5 Million — Unprecedented Displacement
note: IDP numbers surpassed 1.5 million by mid-2021; Sahel and Est regions largely beyond state control. Year and scale confirmed.

title: January Military Coup — Damiba Ousts Kaboré
note: Coup on January 24, 2022 led by Lt. Col. Paul-Henri Sandaogo Damiba; Kaboré arrested. ECOWAS suspended Burkina Faso. All core facts confirmed.

title: Damiba's MPSR Suspends Constitution and Governs by Decree
note: MPSR suspended constitution and dissolved government following the January 2022 coup. Year and facts confirmed.

title: Second Coup Within Months — Traoré Deposes Damiba
note: Captain Ibrahim Traoré ousted Damiba on September 30, 2022. Traoré was 34. All core facts confirmed.

title: Traoré Government Expels French Ambassador and Troops
note: The French ambassador was expelled and French troops given one month to leave in January 2023, not in late 2022. Year is off by one year.

title: Compaoré Convicted In Absentia for Sankara Assassination
note: Compaoré was convicted and sentenced to life in absentia on April 6, 2022, not October 2022. While the year 2022 is correct, the event description references 'October 2022' which is wrong — the verdict was in April 2022. Year 2022 is correct but the implied timing within the year is inaccurate. Marking VERIFIED as the year itself is correct.

title: Wagner Group Mercenaries Deployed — Russia Pivot Solidifies
note: Russian Africa Corps (formerly Wagner) first published images of deployment to Burkina Faso in January 2024, not 2023. Russia-Africa Summit engagement occurred in July 2023 and preparatory steps took place in 2023, but the actual troop deployment was confirmed in early 2024. Year is ambiguous; marking UNVERIFIED.

title: Alliance des États du Sahel — Junta Bloc Formed with Mali and Niger
note: AES (Liptako-Gourma Charter) formally signed on September 16, 2023 by Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. All core facts confirmed.

title: Kafolo-Type Supply Road Siege — Jihadists Blockade Northern Towns
note: JNIM blockades of Djibo, Titao, and other northern towns are well documented from 2022–2023; populations faced starvation conditions. Year 2023 and core facts confirmed.

title: VDP Volunteer Defense Forces Mobilized — Civilian Armed Auxiliaries
note: Traoré's government expanded VDP program aggressively in 2023; UN investigators documented VDP abuses including killings targeting Fulani communities. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: Burkina Faso Formally Withdraws from ECOWAS
note: Burkina Faso sent formal withdrawal notification to ECOWAS in January 2024, not 2023. The AES announcement was in September 2023 but the formal ECOWAS withdrawal notice was January 2024. Year is off by one.

title: Press Freedom Suspended — Independent Radio Stations Shut Down
note: RFI suspended December 2022, France 24 in March 2023, BBC and VOA temporarily suspended in 2024; journalists arrested and some forcibly conscripted. Year 2023 is correct as the main escalation year. Core facts confirmed.

title: IDP Crisis Reaches 2 Million — One of World's Worst
note: IDP numbers exceeded 2 million by 2023; food insecurity affected approximately 4.7 million people. Year and scale confirmed.

title: Traoré Declares Burkina Faso a Sovereign State — New Governance Decree
note: Traoré has made numerous sovereignty declarations and decrees throughout 2023–2024, but a specific landmark sovereignty decree in 2024 with the exact characteristics described (requiring parliamentary approval for foreign military) could not be confirmed from available sources.

title: Elections Postponed Indefinitely — Junta Entrenches Power
note: Elections promised under the transitional charter were postponed with junta citing security crisis; mirrors Mali and Niger. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: Spiraling Insecurity — Over 60 Percent of Territory Beyond State Control
note: By 2024, security analysts estimated over 60% of Burkina Faso's territory was contested or controlled by non-state armed groups. Year and scale consistent with multiple sources.

title: UN Human Rights Office Expelled from Burkina Faso
note: A senior UN official was expelled in 2025 (not 2024); earlier in 2022 Barbara Manzi was declared persona non grata. The specific 2024 expulsion of the entire UN Human Rights Office as described could not be confirmed from available sources.

title: Traoré Joins Niger-Mali Junta Axis — Anti-Western Alliance Consolidates
note: Burkina Faso deepened AES alignment through 2024; AES confederation formally established July 2024; common passport and currency plans announced. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: Upper Volta Joins United Nations
note: Upper Volta was admitted to the United Nations on September 20, 1960, not 1961. Year is off by one year.

title: Drought and Famine Devastate Sahel Region
note: The 1968–1974 Sahel drought devastated Upper Volta and surrounding countries; 1972–74 was the worst phase. Year 1972 is correct as beginning of the worst phase. Core facts confirmed.

title: Labour Migration to Côte d'Ivoire Institutionalized
note: Burkina Faso labor migration to Côte d'Ivoire peaked in the mid-1970s with millions working in Ivorian agriculture under bilateral arrangements. Year and scale confirmed.

title: Ivoirité Crisis Expels Burkinabè Migrants from Côte d'Ivoire
note: The Ivoirité crisis and mass expulsions of Burkinabè from Côte d'Ivoire occurred primarily in 1999–2002 (especially 1999 Tabou conflict and the 2002 civil war), not 1982. Year is materially wrong.

title: Sankara's Environmental Revolution — Tree Planting and Anti-Desertification
note: Sankara's nationwide environmental mobilization and tree-planting program are well documented aspects of his revolutionary period. Year 1984 as representative of this program is consistent.

title: Compaoré Begins Hosting West African Peace Negotiations
note: Compaoré's mediation role began in the late 1980s–1990s but was initially intertwined with supporting rebels in Liberia and Sierra Leone. His formal recognized mediation role developed more robustly in the 1990s–2000s. 1987 start year is plausible but not specifically confirmed.

title: FESPACO Film Festival Becomes Africa's Largest Cinema Event
note: FESPACO has been biennial since 1979 and is recognized as Africa's most prestigious film festival, but no specific source confirms 1994 as the year it 'became' Africa's largest. The festival has been growing continuously since 1969. Year label is arbitrary.

title: IMF Structural Adjustment Deepens Under Compaoré
note: Burkina Faso deepened IMF structural adjustment through the mid-1990s including privatization and trade liberalization. Year 1996 as representative is consistent with sources.

title: HIPC Debt Relief Granted — Development Resources Freed
note: Burkina Faso reached HIPC completion point in July 2000, obtaining significant debt relief. Year and core facts confirmed.

title: GM Cotton Introduced — Agricultural Biotechnology Adoption
note: GM Bt cotton was commercially introduced in Burkina Faso in 2008, not 2004. Field trials ran 2003–2005. Year is off by four years.

title: Sahel Region Violence Begins — First Jihadist Attacks in North
note: First organized attacks in northern Sahel region began in 2015–2016 with Ansarul Islam's first attack in December 2016; some earlier cross-border spillover from Mali did occur from 2015. Year 2014 is slightly early — the first significant attacks were 2015–2016.

title: Ansarul Islam Founded — Local Jihadist Movement Emerges
note: Ansarul Islam was founded in November 2016 by Ibrahim Malam Dicko; first attack claimed December 2016 in Nassoumbou. Year and all core facts confirmed.

title: Inata and Arbinda Attacks — Dozens of Soldiers Killed
note: Arbinda attack on December 24, 2019 killed 7 security forces and 35 civilians; Inata gendarmerie attack referenced in some sources as November 2019 (though the larger Inata massacre was November 2021). Year 2019 confirmed for Arbinda; description is consistent.

title: Inata Gendarmerie Massacre — 57 Security Forces Killed
note: Jihadist attack on Inata gendarmerie post on November 14, 2021 killed 57 people including 53 gendarmes. Post had been undersupplied. All core facts confirmed.
